title: Atomization in Early Elementary Science
author: Olivia Mullins
summary: Olivia Mullins describes atomization, the practice of decomposing material into the smallest necessary units and teaching each new atom explicitly, one at a time. She grounds it in cognitive load theory and Direct Instruction, then works through an eight-step process using the kindergarten science standard on what animals need to survive. The worked example shows how she narrows the objective, lists the gist atoms, flags those likely unfamiliar to 15 percent or more of students, and separates unfamiliar concepts from unfamiliar vocabulary. She even swaps the word survive for live because five-year-olds may not know it. She also identifies nested atoms, such as the fact that many kindergartners do not know that people and insects are animals. She argues that atomization supports sophisticated thinking, matters most for students with less background knowledge, and has a real time cost that curriculum developers rather than individual teachers should carry.
points: Atomization means breaking content into the smallest necessary units and teaching one new atom at a time to mastery, in line with cognitive load theory.
Her eight-step process runs from the lesson objective through gist atoms, unfamiliarity checks, nested atoms and pre-teaching decisions before any teaching starts.
Even simple words matter: she replaces survive with live because many five-year-olds may not yet know the word, and checks for gaps such as not knowing that people and bugs are animals.
Atomization is described as an equity tool because students with low background knowledge are hurt most when foundations are skipped.
The process is time-consuming, so she argues curriculum developers rather than individual teachers should do the full atomizing, while teachers should still understand the ideas.
quotes: Atomization is a term used by some to describe the process of decomposing materials into the smallest necessary units, and ensuring that each new atom is explicitly taught one at a time.

A central principle here is that, in line with cognitive load theory, students should be presented with one new concept, or atom, at a time. Students should gain mastery over each atom before building upon it.
However, focusing on multiple items at once violates the “one new concept at a time" rule that cognitive load demands.
For example, kindergartners know dogs, cats, and elephants are animals, but they often do not know that bugs or people are animals.

It is precisely because we break down the content into manageable pieces that students are able to understand complex concepts and build the foundational knowledge that is essential to higher-order thinking.
Students who come to school with high background knowledge can often get by with curriculum that skips explicitly teaching the foundations. Students without this privilege get left behind
If you want to talk about gap-closing, if you want to talk about equity, then talk about explicit instruction and atomization.

Teachers should not be the ones responsible for atomizing their entire year of content — it’s a time-intensive process. This should be the purview of curriculum developers who ideally provide options for differentiation.
